The (now obsolete) spelling variant ''zettul'' is influenced by from French cédule.}Occasional weak inflection was found in Middle High German and persisted into the 18th century. *Zibbe*German{}|Alternative forms}rare,dialectal,archaic|Etymology}19th century. Probably from or related to from Proto-West Germanic tbitch,female dog,whence also from Middle Low German tēve,from Middle Low German tiffe,from Middle Dutch tēve (13th c.,modern from Dutch teef),from Old English tife.}While the 19th-century attestation is surely belated,the total lack of medieval evidence and the fact that the word is native almost exclusively in East Central German,thus outside the original from Old High German - territory,make its inheritedness from German nocap1. One alternative would be a phonetically adapted borrowing from Low German (during the time of dialect mixing in the colonial areas),plausibly under the influence of from Middle High German tbitch,doe rabbit. *Ziege*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German zige,from Old High German ziga,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆tigā.  was originally found in Franconian dialects alongside otherwise exclusive Geiß. In Middle High German times,it established itself in the colonial dialects (East Central German) and also conquered vast areas of Low German,where the borrowing from Middle Low German sēge was predominant since at least the 15th century (due to a virtual lack of domestic goat breeding). During the same time,curiously,was widely lost in West Central German and Upper Franconian,its original provenance. Its eventual victory in the standard language was reinforced by its use in Luther’s Bible.|Pronunciation}/ˈt͡siːɡə/}De-@^.OGG}Ⓓ7/73/De-@^2.ogg}Zie+ge|Noun}(fem.)}#goat}•synononym:[Geiß (regional)<g:f)],[Hippe (regional)]}#informal a stupid,stubborn person (usually female)}•synononym:Zicke|Usage notes}The singular refers principally to female goats,though it might also be used for male ones. The plural is entirely neutral with regard to natural gender.}The female gender may be specified by means of the word Zicke,which is uncommon in literary German,however.|Derived terms}alte @^n lecken auch gern Salz}@^nbart,@^nbock,@^nfell,@^nficker,@^nkäse,@^nmilch,@^nstall}Angoraziege,Bergziege,Hausziege,Milchziege,Schneeziege,Wildziege,Zimtziege|See also}Bock}Geißbock}Zicke

*Zirkel*German{}''' (monogram),comprised of E,F,V.|Etymology}From Middle High German zirkel,from Old High German zirkil,from Latin tpair of compasses,from Ancient Greek κίρκινος. The Old High German ''-il'' is due to either alteration after the Germanic tool suffix from Proto-Germanic ⋆-ilaz,or confluence with from Latin tcircle; the ''-k-'' speaks in favour of the latter explanation. The sense “circle”,which appears in Middle High German,is at any rate borrowed from Latin circulus. *zwei*Alemannic German{}ain|Alternative forms}zwëi|Etymology}From Middle High German @^,from Old High German @^ (neuter of from Old High German zwēne).}Cognate with from German @^,from Dutch twee,from English two,from Icelandic tveir.|Number}#two}German|Alternative forms}zwey|Etymology}From Middle High German @^,from Old High German @^ (neuter of from Old High German zwēne).}Compare from Dutch twee,from English two,from English twain. In Old High German,and still today in some dialects,distinct forms are used for the three grammatical genders. ''Zwei'' was originally the neuter form,now used for all genders. The Old High German masculine from Old High German zwēne is found back in early modern from German zween; the feminine from Old High German zwō lives on in the variant zwo (but now without any gender distinction).|Pronunciation}/t͡svaɪ̯/+t͡sʋaɪ̯}Ⓓ2/27/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ2/2e/De-@^2.ogg}/t͡svo/,(regionally)}Rhymes:aɪ̯|Numeral}#cardinal two Literally:[numerical value represented by the Arabic numeral 2; or ''describing a set with two components'']}•synononym:zwo|Coordinate terms}de-cardinals|Derived terms}Zweiklang}Zweiweg- (Gleichrichter)|See also}Silesian ees,zwee,drei,vier,fimf,sechs,siem,acht,neun,zahn,elf,zwelf

*zwingen*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German twingen,from Old High German dwingan,from Proto-Germanic ⋆þwinganą,from Proto-Germanic ⋆þwinhaną,related to from Proto-Germanic clamp,strap.}Cognates include from Dutch dwingen,from Norwegian tvinge,from Swedish tvinga,from Icelandic þvinga. What may be perceived as a repetition of the consonant shift (from Germanic ''}þ'' → Old High German ''d'' → Middle High German ''t'' → modern German ''z'') is a regular development that affected most words with Old High German ''dw-'' and ''tw-'' (compare Zwerg,but see also quengeln for a counterexample). *ᛉ*German{},Germany.|Etymology}From the interpretation as Lebensrune.|Symbol}from German symbol}#obsolete born (replacing})}•from German ᛦ
*ᛦ*German{},Germany.}.|Etymology}From the interpretation as Todesrune.|Symbol}#obsolete died,dead (replacing †)}•ᛉ|Usage notes}The rune is part of the w:Armanen runes,which are based on the Younger Futhark. The visual representation of the rune in the original publication is closer to ⟨ᛣ⟩,with straight arms to mirror ⟨ᛉ⟩,but this denotes a different letter,m+:calc IPAchar:/k/,and not ''yr''. There is currently no specific codepoint in Unicode for straight-armed ''yr'' as opposed to curved-armed ''yr'',so both are conventionally encoded as ⟨&_⟩. It should be noted that the distinction between round and straight runes is purely graphemic,and not historically something that distinguishes one runic script from another.

A*Ä*German{}|&_lternative forms}lowercase|Etymology}letter From &_lemannic from Middle High German aͤ,a representation of secondary umlaut æ. In Early Modern German,the letter spread to Central German,which did not have a special phoneme for secondary umlaut. Therefore,was seen there as a marker of umlaut as such,and was used analogously.}sound from Middle High German - distinguished up to five stressed e-vowels:æ,ɛ,ɛː,e,eː. Through open-syllable lengthening,mergers,and analogy,this system was not just reduced but entirely altered. 19th-century Standard German generally retained only one short vowel,but distinguished ɛː from eː. &_ll long ⟨ä⟩s were by then usually pronounced ɛː,while ⟨e⟩ was ɛː in some words,eː in others. The choice between these,however,varied greatly from region to region,and was entirely absent in many Low German areas. Theodor Siebs therefore (consistently but rather arbitrarily) restricted ɛː to the spelling ⟨ä⟩ in his codification of stage and broadcasting German. Unintendedly,this reinforced the tendency towards total merger as the dialectal systems of distinction were disturbed.|Pronunciation}/ɛː/+/ˌaː ˈʊmlaʊ̯t/letter name}Ⓓ2/2e/De-%C3%84.ogg}/ɛ/short phoneme}/ɛː/+ɛː+eː long phoneme}The distinction between long IP&_char:/ɛː/and IP&_char:/eː/is maintained in some regions,including Switzerland and most of western Germany. In many other regions the two are merged in normal speech,though speakers may nevertheless distinguish them in individual words (such as conditional forms of strong verbs,e.g.,gäbe) and in enunciation. This usually also includes the monosyllabic pronunciation of the letter name ⟨&~⟩ itself.}Rhymes:eː one pronunciation}E one pronunciation|Letter}(neut.,genitive:&~s,plural:[&~s][s])}#a letter used in German spelling:most often an umlauted version of &_#German+&_

Ahre*Ähre*German{}|Alternative forms}obsolete|Etymology}From Middle High German eher,from Middle High German gn,from Old High German ehir,from Old High German ahir,from Old High German gn,from Proto-Germanic gn. The form with ''Ä-'' is Upper German,where ''-h-'' led to an open vowel through secondary (rather than primary) umlaut. The feminine form,in turn,is a chiefly Central German backformation from plural use.}Cognate with from Dutch aar,from West Frisian ier,from English ear. ^ö*aus dem Grobsten heraus*German{}|Prepositional phrase}#colloquial out of the woods}•synononym:über den Berg}#}• Freilich hat der Virologe Christian Drosten zu den Schutzmaßnahmen noch gar nichts gesagt. Geäußert hat er Folgendes:Dass „wir nach diesem Winter“ '''^@''' sein werden. Der Winter endet bekanntlich nicht Anfang Januar  sondern im März. (Although the virologist Christian Drosten has yet to comment on the protective measures)  he has indeed made a statement:"After this winter season we will be '''out of the woods'''." Note that the winter season does not typically conclude in early January  but rather in March.

Befahigung zum Richteramt*Befähigung zum Richteramt*German{}|Noun}(fem.)}#Germany the status of a person who qualifies for practice as an attorney,state attorney,or judge due to either having completed legal education with the successful first and second state examinations (Volljurist) or being a professor ordinarius of law (which only requires the first state examination,alone however empirically rare for a professor of law). Such persons also qualify for all levels of public administration as civil servants in the same fashion as those master's level graduates who have completed preparatory service (Referendariat) specific to public administration.
